Prevention: Controlling this soil-borne disease is very difficult and largely depends on good soil management:
Incorporate compost or manure into soil
Control soil pH; use limestone to increase soil pH to 6-7
Control root-knot nematodes as they aggravate the disease
Avoid movement of tools/equipment/water from infested to non- infested soils
Change planting date to avoid high soil temperature (>24 °C) and high soil moisture
Before planting, solarize the nursey beds by applying a thin sheet of plastic over the soil and leaving the sun to heat the soil for 20-60 days
Graft crop onto resistant rootstocks if available (ex: tomato on resistant aubergine rootstock)
Use tubers (potato) and seeds from crops found disease-free for the last 2 growing seasons
Avoid damaging the roots; roots injured by farm tools and soil pests favour infection
Avoid crop rotation with other host plants: solanaceae crops, groundnut or tobacco
Do not grow susceptible crops in lowlands, wet areas or fields where the disease has occurred
Monitoring: Regularly inspect the fields for symptoms throughout the growing crop from nursery stage through harvest
Rapid wilting of all branches at the same time
The cut stem shows a brown discoloration and white/ yellowish liquid may be released when pressing the stem
Tubers: bacterial ooze emerges from the eyes and stem-end
Browning and necrosis of the vascular ring and in adjacent tissues, and usually a creamy exudate on the vascular ring
Youngest leaves: during the warmest time of the day leaves appear wilted and limp, and then appear to recover at night
After 2-3 days, the whole plant wilts and dies suddenly
In case of slow development of the disease, the plant stunts and produces a lot of roots on the stem
Cut a piece of the stem from the base and suspend it in a glass of water at the water level.
Look for a milky substance streaming into the water
Direct Control: Pull out plants with roots and surrounding soil
Carry the infected material from the field in a sealed plastic bag
Burn or bury (at least 1 meter deep) far enough from the field
Treat soil by incorporating cruciferous plant residues (mustard, broccoli, cabbage, radish, cauliflower, etc) into the soil
Disinfect all farm implements/ tools with bleach after they have been used in infected fields
Practice prolonged flooding in infested fields for a minimum of 6 months
Chemical control is ineffective because this disease is soil-borne
